chief_complaint: growing 2.5 cm ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma on lower lip requiring wide local excision and flap reconstruction
hpi_details: 61F farmer presents with a 6-month history of a non-healing, rough, ulcerated nodule with raised pearly borders on the central right lower lip vermilion border. Complains of occasional bleeding when eating and pain. Biopsy by dermatologist confirmed well-differentiated invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) extending across 40% of the lower lip width.
ideas: thinks years of sun exposure working outdoors caused the lip cancer
concerns: terrified of severe facial disfigurement, drooling, and inability to speak or eat normally after surgery
expectations: wants complete removal of the cancer with the best aesthetic and functional lip reconstruction possible
social_hx: Crop farmer, chronic sun exposure without lip balm SPF, non-smoker

available_results.value: Well-differentiated invasive squamous cell carcinoma extending into the superficial orbicularis oris; no perineural invasion identified in the biopsy

clinical_knowledge.topic: Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lower Lip (Stage II - T2 N0 M0) requiring resection involving >1/3 to 1/2 lip width defect evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lower Lip (Stage II - T2 N0 M0) requiring resection involving >1/3 to 1/2 lip width defect is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Perform wide local full-thickness excision of lower lip lesion with frozen section margin confirmation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: growing 2.5 cm ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma on lower lip requiring wide local excision and flap reconstruction

Key HPI features: 61F farmer presents with a 6-month history of a non-healing, rough, ulcerated nodule with raised pearly borders on the central right lower lip vermilion border. Complains of occasional bleeding when eating and pain. Biopsy by dermatologist confirmed well-differentiated invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) extending across 40% of the lower lip width.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 72, BP 134/82. Examination reveals a 2.5 x 1.8 cm indurated, central-right lower lip ulceration involving the vermilion and cutaneous junction with infiltration into underlying orbicularis oris muscle. Palpation of submental and submandibular neck triangles reveals no cervical lymphadenopathy (cN0). Wide local excision with 5 mm histological margins will result in a full-thickness defect encompassing ~45% of the lower lip.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lower Lip (Stage II - T2 N0 M0) requiring resection involving >1/3 to 1/2 lip width defect.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Flap ischemia or tissue necrosis.
management_principles: Perform wide local full-thickness excision of lower lip lesion with frozen section margin confirmation

Given defect size is 45% (between 1/3 and 2/3 of lip width), reconstruct using a full-thickness lip-switch axial pedicled flap (Karapandzic local advancement-rotation flap or Abbe cross-lip flap from upper lip) to preserve oral competence, orbicularis oris motor function, and aesthetic vermilion alignment
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 61F presenting with biopsy-proven invasive squamous cell carcinoma involving 40% of the lower lip requiring oncological resection and functional reconstruction.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 72, BP 134/82. Examination reveals a 2.5 x 1.8 cm indurated, central-right lower lip ulceration involving the vermilion and cutaneous junction with infiltration into underlying orbicularis oris muscle. Palpation of submental and submandibular neck triangles reveals no cervical lymphadenopathy (cN0). Wide local excision with 5 mm histological margins will result in a full-thickness defect encompassing ~45% of the lower lip.
reference_soap.assessment: Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lower Lip (Stage II - T2 N0 M0) requiring resection involving >1/3 to 1/2 lip width defect.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm pathology and complete regional-node assessment before definitive treatment. A head-and-neck/oncologic surgery team should plan margin-controlled excision and select reconstruction according to the confirmed defect, oral competence, staging, and patient goals; arrange surveillance for recurrence and nodal disease.

learning_objectives: Evaluate facial cutaneous malignancy excision margins according to tumor histology, grading, and anatomical location
Classify lip reconstruction ladders based on defect width (<1/3 primary closure, 1/3 to 2/3 Abbe/Estlander/Karapandzic flaps, >2/3 Bernard-Burow or free tissue transfer)
Understand the neurovascular anatomy of the superior and inferior labial arteries and facial nerve branches in lip reconstruction
Outline goals of functional lip restoration: oral sphincter competence, sensory/motor preservation, and vermilion border alignment

must_ask.objective: Sun exposure and risk factor history
must_ask.say: Do you spend a lot of time outdoors, and have you ever smoked or used tobacco?
How long has this sore been on your lip, and has it been growing or changing?
Is the sore painful, and does it bleed when you eat or when your lip is touched?
Have you noticed any new lumps or swelling in your neck or under your jaw?

must_ask.objective: Prior skin lesions or precancerous history
must_ask.say: Have you ever had actinic keratosis or other skin growths removed before?

history.answer: I have this rough sore on my lower lip that started about six months ago, and it keeps growing and won't heal.
I first noticed a tiny rough scaly spot on my lip about six months ago, and it never healed up.
It is located on the middle and right side of my lower lip, right where the pink lip meets the skin.
It started out small like a pimple, but over the past few months it has steadily gotten bigger to about the size of a coin.
It is just this one sore on my lower lip; I do not have any other lumps or lesions anywhere else.
It feels hard and thick when I touch it, and it feels stuck tight to the lip rather than moving freely.
It aches with a stinging pain, especially when I touch it or stretch my mouth to eat.
It regularly crusts over, and then the scab cracks and bleeds whenever I eat or wipe my mouth.
It has raised, rolled pearly edges with a sunken, raw-looking sore in the center.
The skin right around the sore looks irritated and red, but there is no foul-smelling drainage or yellow pus.
I have never tried to squeeze it, and there has never been any cheesy or white paste coming out of it.
No, it stays large and swollen all the time; it does not shrink or fluctuate with rest.
I have never had any cuts, surgery, piercings, or cold sores in that exact spot on my lip.
Eating has become quite difficult because chewing stretches the lip and causes bleeding, and hot or salty foods sting badly.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss.
I have felt around my jawline and neck, and I have not noticed any swollen glands or lumps there.
I have worked outdoors as a crop farmer for over thirty years under intense sunlight, and I never used sunscreen or sunblock lip balm.
Yes, over my decades of farm work I have had many bad blistering sunburns on my face and shoulders.
My dermatologist has frozen off several rough, precancerous sun spots from my cheeks and forehead over the years.
My dermatologist took a small biopsy of this lip sore two weeks ago and told me it is squamous cell carcinoma, which is why I was sent here for surgery.
I think spending decades out in the blazing sun without protecting my lips is what caused this skin cancer.
I am terrified that removing it will leave my face disfigured, or that I will end up drooling and unable to speak clearly.
I hope the surgeon can take out all of the cancer completely while rebuilding my lip so that it looks and works as normally as possible.
I have high blood pressure and sun-damaged skin, but I do not have diabetes, liver disease, or kidney problems.
I have never had any major operations or hospitalizations, just the biopsy of my lip two weeks ago.
I take amlodipine 5 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure. I do not take any over-the-counter pills or herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
I do not drink alcohol, aside from maybe half a glass of beer once a year at harvest time.
I work as a vegetable and crop farmer, and I live in a rural farming house with my husband.
No one in my family has had skin cancer or any other type of cancer; my parents only had high blood pressure.
I went through menopause naturally ten years ago when I was fifty-one, and I have had no bleeding since.

exam.finding: Alert, well-appearing woman in no acute distress with noticeable chronic solar elastosis on the face.
Blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and temperature is 36.6 degrees Celsius.

Inspection and palpation of the lower lip reveal a 2.5 by 1.8 cm indurated, ulcerated lesion on the central-right vermilion-cutaneous border infiltrating into the underlying orbicularis oris muscle with localized tenderness.
Palpation of the submental, submandibular, and anterior and posterior cervical lymph node chains reveals no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.
Total body skin inspection reveals scattered rough, erythematous actinic keratoses on the sun-exposed face and dorsal forearms, with no other suspicious nodules or malignant lesions.
Facial sensation across all three branches including the bilateral mental nerves is fully intact, and lower lip motor tone is preserved without weakness.
Normal S1 and S2 present with regular rate and rhythm and no murmurs or extra heart sounds.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing or crackles.
